subject: Science
source: Drive: Schemes of work Science 'science KS3 SOW' (breathing and respiration, chemical reactions, forces and motion strands), National Curriculum KS3 Science (Edexcel-aligned)

lessons.title: The breathing system
objectives: Name the main parts of the human breathing system
Explain how the diaphragm and rib muscles move air in and out
Use a model to explain ventilation and its limitations

keywords.def: the movement of air into and out of the lungs
the windpipe that carries air to the lungs
tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange happens
a sheet of muscle below the lungs that helps us breathe

starter: Bismillah. Name two nutrients and one job each does (Year 8 recall).
Which gas do our cells need from the air?
Name an organ in the body and say what its job is.

teach.heading: Why do we breathe?
bullets: Cells need oxygen to release energy from food
Breathing brings oxygen in and takes carbon dioxide out
Breathing is not the same as respiration
teach.note: Bismillah. Start by asking pupils to hold their breath for as long as is comfortable and notice the urge to breathe. Explain that the urge is triggered by carbon dioxide building up, not lack of oxygen. Clarify the difference: breathing (ventilation) moves air; respiration is the chemical reaction in cells, which we study in lesson 7. Allah has made this process automatic so we keep breathing even while asleep.

teach.heading: Parts of the breathing system
bullets: Air enters through nose or mouth, then the trachea
Trachea splits into two bronchi, then many bronchioles
Bronchioles end in alveoli inside the lungs
Ribs protect the lungs; the diaphragm lies below them
teach.note: Draw or screen-share a labelled diagram and have pupils label a blank copy. Point out that the trachea has rings of cartilage that keep it open. Lungs have no muscle of their own, so they cannot pump air; this is a common misconception worth raising. Ask: why are the lungs inside the ribcage?

teach.heading: Breathing in (inhaling)
bullets: Diaphragm contracts and moves down
Intercostal muscles contract and lift the ribs up and out
Volume of the chest increases
Pressure falls, so air is pushed in from outside
teach.note: Stress that air is pushed in by the higher pressure outside, it is not sucked in by the lungs. Pupils can place hands on their lower ribs and feel them move up and out. Ask: what happens to the chest volume? Link volume and pressure: more space means lower pressure.

teach.heading: Breathing out (exhaling)
bullets: Diaphragm relaxes and moves up into a dome
Intercostal muscles relax and ribs move down and in
Chest volume decreases
Pressure rises, so air is pushed out
teach.note: Ask pupils to compare with inhaling using a two-column table. Mention that during exercise we also use abdominal and rib muscles to force air out faster. Misconception: pupils say lungs 'fill up' like balloons by themselves; they are passive and follow chest movements.

teach.heading: The bell jar model
bullets: Plastic bottle, balloon and sheet of rubber make a lung model
Pulling the rubber down lowers pressure and the balloon inflates
The model shows pressure and volume changes
Limitations: no ribs, no real tubes, not moist
teach.note: Home version: cut the bottom off a plastic bottle, put a balloon inside the neck, stretch another balloon over the cut end. Pull down and watch the inner balloon inflate. Ask pupils to evaluate the model: what does it represent (balloon = lungs, rubber = diaphragm) and what is missing? Take care when cutting; an adult should do it.

practice: Name the tube that carries air from the mouth to the lungs.
Does the diaphragm move up or down when we breathe in?
Explain why air enters the lungs when the chest volume increases.
independent: Draw and label the breathing system with seven labels and one function each.
Make a flow chart of inhaling: diaphragm, ribs, volume, pressure, air.
Make a flow chart of exhaling and compare with inhaling in a table.
Evaluate the lung model: give two strengths and two weaknesses.
exit: Which two muscle groups are used in breathing?
What happens to the pressure inside the chest during inhaling?
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled diagram of the breathing system and write a caption explaining how air gets into the lungs.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters and a pre-labelled diagram with a word bank. EAL: pre-teach 'inhale' and 'exhale' with actions. Stretch: explain using particle ideas why a lower pressure inside the chest draws air in.

lessons.title: Chemical reactions and conservation of mass
objectives: Describe the signs that a chemical reaction has taken place
Distinguish chemical changes from physical changes
Explain why mass is conserved in a closed system and use this to predict masses

keywords.def: a substance that is used up in a chemical reaction
a new substance made in a chemical reaction
a change where no new substance is made, such as melting
the total mass stays the same during a reaction

starter: Bismillah. Name an element and a compound.
What is the difference between an atom and a molecule?
What is a mixture? Give one example.

teach.heading: Physical or chemical change?
bullets: Physical: melting, freezing, dissolving; easy to reverse
Chemical: a new substance is made; usually hard to reverse
Chemical changes are called chemical reactions
teach.note: Hold up examples (screen or real): ice melting, wax burning, sugar dissolving, bread toasting. Pupils vote physical or chemical and justify. Misconception: dissolving is a chemical change. Point out that evaporating the water returns the sugar.

teach.heading: Signs of a chemical reaction
bullets: Bubbles of gas are given off
Colour change
Temperature change
A solid (precipitate) forms or a flame is seen
teach.note: These are clues, not proof. Boiling also gives bubbles, and a colour change might be physical. A new substance is the real test. Safe home demonstration: vinegar and bicarbonate of soda give bubbles of carbon dioxide and the mixture gets slightly colder. Ask pupils to identify the evidence.

teach.heading: Reactants and products
bullets: Reactants are on the left, products on the right
Written as a word equation: reactants → products
Example: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide
Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed
teach.note: Show the burning of magnesium ribbon (video) giving a bright white light and white ash. Explain that the same atoms are there before and after, just joined differently. Ask: which are the reactants? Which is the product? Link to Qur'an 55:7-9, which stresses that the heavens were set up with balance; conservation laws show the order in creation.

teach.heading: Conservation of mass
bullets: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products
Atoms are not lost or gained
In an open container, gases can escape so mass appears to change
Example: 24 g Mg + 16 g O gives 40 g MgO
teach.note: Worked example: 24 g of magnesium reacts with 16 g of oxygen. Mass of magnesium oxide = 24 + 16 = 40 g. Ask pupils to predict what happens to the mass when magnesium burns in an open crucible (it increases, because oxygen from the air is added). This is a very common exam question.

teach.heading: The disappearing mass puzzle
bullets: A fizzing tablet in an open flask appears to lose mass
The carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air
In a sealed flask the mass stays constant
Mass lost = mass of gas given off
teach.note: Example: a flask and contents has mass 150.0 g. After the reaction in the open, it reads 149.2 g. The gas had mass 0.8 g. Ask: how could we prove the mass is conserved? (Seal the flask, use a balloon over the top.) Mention that gases have mass, which many pupils doubt.

practice: Name two signs that a chemical reaction has happened.
What are the reactants in: hydrogen + oxygen → water?
Is melting wax a physical or chemical change? Explain.
independent: Sort 10 changes (e.g. rusting, boiling water, baking a cake, dissolving salt) into physical or chemical and justify each.
In a reaction 12 g of carbon reacts with 32 g of oxygen. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide made.
A flask loses 1.5 g during a fizzing reaction in an open flask. Explain why.
Explain why a piece of iron wool gets heavier when it rusts.
exit: State the law of conservation of mass in your own words.
In a reaction 10 g of A reacts with 6 g of B. What is the total mass of products?
lessons.homework: Observe one chemical change at home (such as toast or an effervescent tablet in water) and write a paragraph naming reactants, products and evidence.
lessons.send: SEND: use a sorting card activity with pictures. EAL: pre-teach 'reactant' and 'product' with a visual. Stretch: explain why mass appears to increase when magnesium burns in an open crucible.

lessons.title: Speed
objectives: Define speed and use speed = distance ÷ time
Convert between km/h and m/s
Distinguish average speed from instantaneous speed

keywords.def: how far an object travels in a given time
total distance divided by total time
how far an object has moved, in metres or kilometres
metres per second, the SI unit of speed

starter: Bismillah. What are the units of length and time?
Convert 2.5 km into metres.
Work out 150 ÷ 6.

teach.heading: What is speed?
bullets: Speed tells us how fast something is moving
speed = distance ÷ time
Units: metres per second (m/s) or km/h
Speed has size only, no direction
teach.note: Ask pupils: which is faster, a cheetah or a car on a motorway? Introduce speed as a rate. Make sure pupils know the formula triangle: D on top, S and T below. Note that velocity is speed with direction, which is for later.

teach.heading: Using the equation
bullets: Worked example: 120 m in 15 s
speed = 120 ÷ 15 = 8 m/s
Rearrange: distance = speed × time
Rearrange: time = distance ÷ speed
teach.note: Model setting out: write the equation, substitute, calculate, add the unit. Do two more examples: a car travels 90 km in 1.5 h (60 km/h); how far does a cyclist travelling at 6 m/s go in 40 s (240 m)? Insist on units each time.

teach.heading: Average and instantaneous speed
bullets: Journeys have stops and starts
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time
Instantaneous speed is the speed at one moment
A speedometer shows instantaneous speed
teach.note: Example: a bus travels 30 km in 1 h, then waits 30 min, then travels 30 km in 1 h. Total distance 60 km in 2.5 h gives 24 km/h. Ask pupils why the average is lower than the speed shown on the speedometer while moving. Misconception: average speed is the mean of the speeds. It is not always.

teach.heading: Changing units
bullets: km/h to m/s: divide by 3.6
m/s to km/h: multiply by 3.6
Example: 72 km/h = 20 m/s
Convert to the same units before calculating
teach.note: Derive the 3.6: 1 km/h = 1000 m ÷ 3600 s. Practise: 54 km/h = 15 m/s; 5 m/s = 18 km/h. Pupils often forget to convert minutes to seconds as well. Keep the units consistent and cross-check that the answer is sensible.

teach.heading: Typical speeds
bullets: Walking: about 1.5 m/s
Cycling: about 6 m/s
Car on a motorway: about 30 m/s
Sound in air: about 340 m/s; light: 300 000 000 m/s
teach.note: Use these for estimation and to build a sense of scale. Ask: how long does light from the Sun take to reach us? Roughly 500 s (8 minutes) by 150 000 000 km ÷ 300 000 km/s. Optional extension. Remind pupils about safe, legal speed limits as a matter of caring for others: protecting life is an amanah.

practice: A runner covers 100 m in 12.5 s. Calculate the speed.
A train travels at 40 m/s for 30 s. Calculate the distance.
How long does it take to cycle 3000 m at 6 m/s?
independent: Complete a table of six speed calculations with different missing quantities.
Convert 90 km/h into m/s and 12 m/s into km/h.
A family drives 180 km in 2 h 15 min. Calculate the average speed in km/h.
A sprinter runs 200 m in 25 s and then jogs 100 m in 25 s. Calculate the average speed for the whole run.
exit: Write the equation for speed.
A car travels 150 km in 2 h. What is its average speed?
lessons.homework: Time yourself walking 20 m in your home or garden and calculate your speed in m/s; repeat while walking fast.
lessons.send: SEND: formula triangle and a set of calculation steps. EAL: pre-teach 'per' and 'average'. Stretch: a runner completes the first half of a 10 km run at 10 km/h and the second half at 15 km/h; find the average speed (12 km/h).

lessons.title: Gas exchange in the lungs
objectives: Describe how oxygen and carbon dioxide move across the alveoli
Explain how alveoli are adapted for gas exchange
Compare the composition of inhaled and exhaled air

keywords.def: the swapping of oxygen and carbon dioxide between air and blood
the net movement of particles from high concentration to low concentration
a tiny blood vessel with a very thin wall
the total area of a surface available for exchange

starter: Name the muscle that moves down when we breathe in.
What happens to the chest volume when we breathe out?
Define diffusion using particle ideas.

teach.heading: Inside the alveoli
bullets: Alveoli are tiny air sacs at the ends of bronchioles
Millions of alveoli in each lung
Each is surrounded by capillaries
Gas exchange happens here
teach.note: Show a diagram of a bunch of grapes to represent alveoli. Ask: why is a lung made of millions of tiny sacs and not one big bag? Lead to surface area. Mention that estimates of total alveolar area vary but are often given as around 70 square metres, many times our skin area.

teach.heading: How gases move
bullets: Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the blood
Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli
Diffusion is from high concentration to low concentration
Blood carries oxygen to cells; haemoglobin in red blood cells holds it
teach.note: Use arrows on the board. The blood arriving at the lungs has low oxygen and high carbon dioxide, so the concentration gradients drive diffusion. Misconception: pupils think the lungs 'pull' oxygen. Gases move by diffusion, a passive process that needs no energy from the cell.

teach.heading: Adaptations of the alveoli
bullets: Large surface area from millions of alveoli
Wall is one cell thick for a short diffusion path
Moist lining so gases dissolve
Good blood supply keeps the concentration gradient steep
teach.note: Make a table: feature, how it helps. Ask pupils to predict what happens in a disease where alveoli are damaged (e.g. emphysema): less surface area, slower gas exchange, breathlessness. Link to how structure matches function.

teach.heading: Inhaled and exhaled air
bullets: Inhaled: about 21% oxygen, 0.04% carbon dioxide
Exhaled: about 16% oxygen, 4% carbon dioxide
Nitrogen is about 78% in both
Exhaled air is also warmer and moister
teach.note: Misconception: exhaled air contains no oxygen. Show it has 16%, which is why rescue breaths can work. Ask pupils to calculate the percentage change in carbon dioxide (a 100-fold increase). Show a video of limewater turning cloudy when exhaled air is bubbled through it; do not use limewater at home.

teach.heading: Fog on a mirror
bullets: Exhaled air contains water vapour
It condenses on a cold surface
Simple home test for water in breath
Water also comes from respiration in cells
teach.note: Pupils can breathe onto a mirror or a window to see fog. Ask where the water vapour comes from. Answer: cell respiration makes water, and the moist surfaces of the lungs add more. This also sets up the equation for aerobic respiration in lesson 7.

practice: Name the tiny air sacs where gas exchange takes place.
Which gas diffuses from the blood into the alveoli?
State the percentage of oxygen in inhaled air.
independent: Complete a table with four alveoli features and an explanation of how each helps.
Draw an alveolus and capillary with arrows showing oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Calculate how many times more carbon dioxide is in exhaled air (4%) than in inhaled air (0.04%).
Explain why a person with damaged alveoli feels out of breath.
exit: Describe how oxygen moves from the alveoli to the blood.
Give two features that make alveoli good for gas exchange.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph titled 'Why my lungs are made of millions of tiny air sacs', using the words surface area and diffusion.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled diagram plus sentence frames (The wall is thin, so...). EAL: pre-teach 'diffuse' and 'concentration' with a perfume example. Stretch: link the adaptations of alveoli to those of the small intestine villi from Year 8.

lessons.title: Word and symbol equations
objectives: Write word equations for reactions
Use chemical symbols and formulae in simple symbol equations
Balance a simple equation by adjusting the numbers in front

keywords.def: chemical symbols showing which atoms are in a substance and in what numbers
a way of showing a reaction using the names of the substances
a way of showing a reaction using formulae
an equation with the same number of each atom on both sides

starter: Write the symbols for oxygen, hydrogen and carbon.
How many atoms are in the formula H2O?
State the law of conservation of mass.

teach.heading: Word equations
bullets: Reactants → products
Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide
Methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
Hydrogen + oxygen → water
teach.note: Revise using the arrow to mean 'react to make'. Ask pupils to write word equations for: iron reacting with sulfur to form iron sulfide, and sodium reacting with chlorine. Reinforce spelling of chemical names, and the idea that 'ide' endings come from two elements.

teach.heading: Symbols and formulae
bullets: Elements: Mg, O2, H2, N2, Cl2
Compounds: H2O, CO2, MgO, NaCl, CH4
Small numbers show how many atoms are joined
Numbers in front show how many molecules
teach.note: Teach the difference between the subscript and the big number in front: O2 is one molecule with two atoms, 2O would be two separate atoms. Ask pupils to count the atoms in: CO2 (3), H2SO4 (7), 2H2O (6). Gases O2, H2, N2, Cl2 exist as pairs.

teach.heading: Writing a symbol equation
bullets: Step 1: write the word equation
Step 2: replace names with formulae
Step 3: count atoms on each side
Example: Mg + O2 → MgO is not balanced
teach.note: Model with magnesium burning. Count: left has 2 O, right has 1 O. Do not change the formulae. Misconception: pupils change subscripts to balance, writing MgO2. Emphasise that we only add numbers in front. This is key to Year 10 and 11 chemistry.

teach.heading: Balancing the equation
bullets: Add a 2 in front of MgO: 2 O on each side
Now Mg is unbalanced, so add 2 in front of Mg
2Mg + O2 → 2MgO
Check: 2 Mg and 2 O on each side
teach.note: Walk through slowly using a tally table: element, left, right. Pupils should check after each step. Qur'an 99:7-8 reminds us that even an atom's weight of good will be seen; use as a reflection on accountability and accuracy, noting no atom is lost in a reaction.

teach.heading: More examples
bullets: H2 + O2 → H2O becomes 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O
CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O
Balance one element at a time
Balance oxygen last when it is by itself
teach.note: Give pupils one minute to attempt hydrogen with oxygen before revealing. For methane, count C(1,1), H(4,2→ add 2 in front of H2O to make 4), O (2,4 → add 2 in front of O2). Pupils should check each atom at the end. Common mistake: forgetting to multiply the whole formula by the big number.

practice: Write a word equation for the reaction of sodium with chlorine to form sodium chloride.
How many oxygen atoms are in 3CO2?
Is H2 + Cl2 → HCl balanced? Explain.
independent: Write word equations for: iron + sulfur; zinc + oxygen; hydrogen + chlorine.
Balance: Mg + O2 → MgO; H2 + O2 → H2O; Na + Cl2 → NaCl.
Balance: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + H2O.
Explain why we must not change the small numbers when balancing.
exit: Balance the equation: Ca + O2 → CaO.
Count the atoms of each element in 2H2O.
lessons.homework: Balance these three equations and show the atom counts: Zn + O2 → ZnO; H2 + Cl2 → HCl; Al + O2 → Al2O3 (stretch).
lessons.send: SEND: use magnetic or paper atom cut-outs to model the equation. EAL: symbols and word bank on a card. Stretch: balance Al + O2 → Al2O3 (4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3).

lessons.title: Distance-time graphs
objectives: Plot and read distance-time graphs
Describe motion from the shape of a graph
Calculate speed from the gradient

keywords.def: a graph showing how far an object has travelled over time
how steep a line is: change in y divided by change in x
not moving
moving at the same speed all the time

starter: Calculate the speed of a car that travels 200 m in 8 s.
Convert 36 km/h to m/s.
How do we work out the gradient of a straight line?

teach.heading: Axes and plotting
bullets: Time goes on the horizontal (x) axis
Distance goes on the vertical (y) axis
Plot points then join with a ruler or smooth line
Always label axes with units
teach.note: Show a table of results for a cyclist: 0 s, 0 m; 10 s, 40 m; 20 s, 80 m; 30 s, 120 m. Ask pupils to plot it. Teach the independent variable on the x-axis. Remind them that scales must be even and fill most of the graph.

teach.heading: Reading the shape
bullets: Straight sloping line: constant speed
Steeper line: faster
Horizontal line: stationary
Line sloping down: returning to the start
teach.note: Draw four small graphs and ask pupils to act them out with arm movements. Misconception: a horizontal line means moving at constant speed (it means stopped). Another: the graph is a picture of the path. It is not.

teach.heading: Gradient equals speed
bullets: Gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time
Draw a triangle on the straight part
Example: 80 m in 20 s gives 4 m/s
Steeper gradient means higher speed
teach.note: Show how to choose two points far apart on the line for accuracy. Do an example: from (10 s, 40 m) to (30 s, 120 m): 80 ÷ 20 = 4 m/s. The gradient is the same as the equation speed = distance ÷ time. Ask pupils to compare with the last lesson.

teach.heading: A journey with stages
bullets: Stage A: 0 to 100 s, 0 to 300 m
Stage B: 100 to 200 s, stopped at 300 m
Stage C: 200 to 300 s, 300 m to 600 m
Speed in A: 3 m/s; B: 0; C: 3 m/s
teach.note: Draw this graph and have pupils describe each stage in a sentence, then calculate the speeds. Ask for the average speed over the whole journey: 600 m ÷ 300 s = 2 m/s. Highlight that average speed differs from the speed in each stage.

teach.heading: Comparing two objects
bullets: Two lines on the same axes
The steeper line is the faster object
Where lines cross they are at the same place at the same time
Check the scale before comparing
teach.note: Example: Ahmad and Yusuf walk to the masjid. Plot both journeys. Ask: who set off later? Who arrived first? When did the faster one overtake? Reference to punctuality for salah: leave in good time to arrive without rushing (walk with calm).

practice: What does a horizontal line on a distance-time graph show?
A line goes from (0, 0) to (10 s, 50 m). Calculate the speed.
Which is faster, a gradient of 2 or 5?
independent: Plot a graph from the table: 0 s, 0 m; 5 s, 10 m; 10 s, 20 m; 15 s, 20 m; 20 s, 40 m.
Describe each stage of the graph and calculate the speed in each.
Calculate the average speed for the whole journey in m/s.
Sketch a graph for a person who walks, stops, then runs back home.
exit: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
A graph goes from (0, 0) to (20 s, 100 m). State the speed.
lessons.homework: Draw a distance-time graph of your journey from your bedroom to the kitchen (estimate distances and times) and describe it.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn axes and a gradient triangle template. EAL: key verbs 'accelerate', 'stop', 'return' with gestures. Stretch: explain what a curved line on a distance-time graph means.

lessons.title: Aerobic respiration
objectives: Define aerobic respiration and state where it happens
Write the word and symbol equations for aerobic respiration
Explain why all living things respire and what energy is used for

keywords.def: a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from food
respiration that uses oxygen
a sugar used as the main fuel for respiration
structures in cells where aerobic respiration takes place

starter: Bismillah. Why do we breathe in oxygen?
Name the products of a reaction in the word equation hydrogen + oxygen → water.
Where do we get glucose from in our diet?

teach.heading: What is respiration?
bullets: Respiration releases energy from glucose
It happens in every living cell, all the time
It is a chemical reaction, not breathing
Plants, animals and fungi all respire
teach.note: Check the misconception first: ask 'Do plants respire?' Many pupils say no. Plants respire day and night; they photosynthesise only in light. Respiration is a continuous process of energy release, like the engine of a car that is always idling. Allah has created cells that are working constantly while we sleep.

teach.heading: The word equation
bullets: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
Energy is released
Oxygen comes from breathing; glucose from food
Carbon dioxide and water leave the body
teach.note: Write the equation in coloured pens and link each part to a body system: oxygen in via lungs and blood, glucose from digestion (Year 8). Use arrows from the lungs, the digestive system and the cells. Ask pupils what happens to the carbon dioxide (breathed out) and water (breath, sweat, urine).

teach.heading: The symbol equation
bullets: Count the atoms: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O each side
It is balanced
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration
teach.note: Use lesson 5 to count atoms: left C6, H12, O (6+12=18); right C 6, H (12), O (12+6=18). Draw a cell with mitochondria and explain that they contain the enzymes. Muscle cells and sperm cells have lots of mitochondria. Ask: why would a muscle cell need many mitochondria?

teach.heading: What is the energy used for?
bullets: Movement through muscle contraction
Keeping warm (about 37°C)
Growth and repair, building proteins
Active transport and sending nerve impulses
teach.note: Ask pupils: why do we feel warm after exercise? Some energy is released as heat, which helps maintain body temperature. Misconception: energy is 'made' in respiration; it is released (transferred) from the chemical energy in glucose. Link: respiration is an exothermic reaction.

teach.heading: Breathing and respiration compared
bullets: Breathing: moving air in and out of lungs
Respiration: chemical reaction in cells
Breathing delivers oxygen for respiration
Respiration gives the energy to power breathing muscles
teach.note: Make a two-column table. Ask: if a person stops breathing, how soon do cells run out of oxygen? Pupils should realise it takes only minutes for the brain. Stress that this is why first aid is so urgent. Mention that Allah created our bodies as an amanah and we should look after them.

practice: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
Where in a cell does aerobic respiration happen?
Why do plants respire as well as photosynthesise?
independent: Draw a diagram showing how oxygen and glucose reach a muscle cell and what leaves it.
Explain three uses of the energy released by respiration.
Count the atoms on each side of C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O to show it is balanced.
Compare breathing with respiration in a table with four rows.
exit: State the word equation for aerobic respiration.
Give two uses of energy in the body.
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph answering: 'A plant does not move or breathe, so why does it need respiration?'
lessons.send: SEND: coloured cards to match equation parts. EAL: pre-teach 'release' and 'fuel'. Stretch: explain why sports people have more mitochondria in their muscle cells.

lessons.title: Acids, alkalis and the pH scale
objectives: Describe acids and alkalis and give examples of each
Use indicators and the pH scale to classify solutions
Describe safety hazards and apply hazard symbols

keywords.def: a substance with a pH below 7 that turns litmus red
a soluble base with a pH above 7 that turns litmus blue
a substance that changes colour depending on pH
a scale from 0 to 14 that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is

starter: Bismillah. Name a mixture and a compound.
Give one sign that a chemical reaction has taken place.
Name a food or drink that tastes sour.

teach.heading: Acids and alkalis around us
bullets: Acids: lemon juice, vinegar, stomach acid, fizzy drinks
Alkalis: soap, bleach, oven cleaner, baking soda solution
Acids taste sour; alkalis feel slippery
Never taste or touch unknown chemicals
teach.note: Ask pupils to list acids and alkalis at home. Emphasise safety: some are corrosive. Mention that stomach acid is hydrochloric acid with pH about 1-2, strong enough to break down food and kill microbes. Misconception: all acids are dangerous. Citric acid in lemons is safe to eat, while bleach is not safe to touch.

teach.heading: Indicators
bullets: Litmus: red in acid, blue in alkali
Universal indicator shows a range of colours
Red cabbage water is a natural indicator
An indicator shows if a substance is acid or alkaline
teach.note: Home practical (adult supervision): boil chopped red cabbage in water, cool, and add to lemon juice, vinegar, bicarbonate of soda solution and soapy water. The colour changes from red/pink (acid) to purple to blue/green (alkali). Pupils record observations in a table. Do not taste the liquids afterwards.

teach.heading: The pH scale
bullets: pH 0 to 14
pH 7 is neutral (pure water)
Below 7 is acidic; above 7 is alkaline
Universal indicator: red (1), green (7), purple (14)
teach.note: Draw a number line with colours. Place examples: stomach acid pH 1, lemon juice 2, vinegar 3, water 7, blood about 7.4, baking soda solution 9, bleach 12, drain cleaner 14. Ask: what does a pH of 3 tell us? A pH of 11? The further from 7, the stronger.

teach.heading: Concentrated and strong
bullets: Concentrated: lots of acid in a small volume of water
Dilute: a little acid in lots of water
A dilute solution can be less harmful
Hazard symbols warn us about corrosive and irritant chemicals
teach.note: Make a distinction between strong/weak (extent of ionisation: GCSE) and concentrated/dilute (amount dissolved). At KS3 stay with concentrated and dilute. Show the corrosive and irritant symbols. Ask: why do we wear eye protection in science? It is part of caring for the body that Allah entrusted to us.

teach.heading: Acids and alkalis in action
bullets: Toothpaste is alkaline: it neutralises acid in the mouth
Rain is naturally slightly acidic, about pH 5.6
Farmers add lime to acidic soil
Indigestion tablets treat too much stomach acid
teach.note: Use well-evidenced examples only: soil pH, toothpaste, antacids and naturally acidic rain (carbon dioxide dissolves in rainwater). Avoid the popular but disputed claims about insect stings. Link to the next lesson on neutralisation. Ask: what do you think happens when you mix an acid and an alkali?

practice: Name the colour of litmus paper in an acid.
What is the pH of a neutral solution?
Is a solution of pH 12 an acid or an alkali?
independent: Make a table of six household substances with predicted pH and acid/alkali/neutral.
Draw the pH scale with colours and place five examples.
Explain the difference between a concentrated and a dilute acid.
Design a fair test to compare the pH of three different drinks using red cabbage indicator.
exit: What does a pH of 2 tell you about a solution?
Name one indicator and give its colour in an alkali.
lessons.homework: Test three household liquids (with an adult) with a natural indicator and record the colour and your pH prediction.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded pH scale on a card. EAL: pre-teach 'acidic', 'alkaline', 'neutral' with samples. Stretch: explain why pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.

lessons.title: Forces and Newton's first law
objectives: State what a force is and give units
Describe contact and non-contact forces
Use force arrows to identify balanced and unbalanced forces

keywords.def: a push or pull measured in newtons (N)
the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting
forces that are equal and opposite, so no change in motion
the unit of force (N)

starter: Bismillah. What is the unit of speed?
Calculate the speed of an object travelling 60 m in 12 s.
What does the gradient of a distance-time graph show?

teach.heading: What is a force?
bullets: A force is a push, pull or twist
Measured in newtons (N) with a newton meter
Forces can change speed, direction or shape
Force is a vector: it has size and direction
teach.note: Show examples: pushing a door, stretching a spring, gravity pulling a ball. Pupils should say what each force does to the object. Introduce the newton meter. Misconception: a moving object needs a force to keep it going. Leave this for the slide on Newton's first law.

teach.heading: Contact and non-contact forces
bullets: Contact: friction, tension, upthrust, air resistance, normal force
Non-contact: gravity, magnetic, electrostatic
Forces act in pairs between objects
Draw each force as an arrow from the object
teach.note: Ask pupils to put these into a Venn diagram. Use the example of a book on a table: weight acts down (gravity) and the table pushes up (normal/reaction force). Arrow length shows the size of the force, and arrow direction shows where it acts.

teach.heading: Force diagrams
bullets: Draw the object as a box or dot
Arrows start from the object
Longer arrow means bigger force
Label each arrow with its name and size
teach.note: Model: a boy pushing a box with 50 N, friction 30 N. Resultant = 50 - 30 = 20 N forwards. Another: a car with a driving force of 800 N and drag of 800 N has a resultant of 0 N. Ask: is the car stopped? (not necessarily; it could be at constant speed).

teach.heading: Balanced and unbalanced forces
bullets: Balanced: resultant is 0 N
Unbalanced: resultant not zero
Unbalanced forces change motion: speed up, slow down or turn
Resultant is the difference when forces oppose
teach.note: Use tug of war on the board. Teams pulling 300 N and 300 N have no change; 350 N vs 300 N gives 50 N resultant to the stronger team. Draw an object at rest and at constant speed; both have balanced forces. Pupils often say a stationary object has no forces. It has balanced forces.

teach.heading: Newton's first law
bullets: An object at rest stays at rest if forces are balanced
A moving object keeps the same speed and direction if forces are balanced
A resultant force changes the motion
Example: seat belts protect passengers when a car stops suddenly
teach.note: Explain inertia: objects resist change. In a car crash, the car stops but passengers continue at their original speed, which is why seat belts matter. Ask: why does a spacecraft far from planets keep moving without engines? Misconception: forces are needed to keep things moving. Friction is the reason things slow down on Earth.

practice: What unit is used to measure force?
Give one example of a non-contact force.
A force of 20 N pushes right and 20 N left. What is the resultant?
independent: Draw force diagrams for: a book resting on a table; a car moving at constant speed; a parachutist speeding up.
Calculate the resultant force when 80 N forwards and 30 N backwards act on a trolley.
Explain, using Newton's first law, why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes.
Sort 10 forces into contact and non-contact in a table.
exit: What does a resultant force of 0 N mean for the motion of an object?
Draw a force diagram for a book at rest on a table.
lessons.homework: Find three objects at home and draw a force diagram for each at rest, naming each force.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn objects with arrows to label. EAL: key words 'push', 'pull', 'balanced' with pictures. Stretch: explain why a skydiver can fall at constant speed even though gravity still acts.

lessons.title: Anaerobic respiration
objectives: Define anaerobic respiration and when it happens
Write word equations for anaerobic respiration in muscles and in yeast
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration

keywords.def: respiration without oxygen, releasing less energy
a substance made in muscles during anaerobic respiration
anaerobic respiration in yeast that makes ethanol and carbon dioxide
the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid

starter: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
Where does aerobic respiration take place?
Why do muscles need energy?

teach.heading: Respiration without oxygen
bullets: Happens when oxygen is in short supply
It releases much less energy than aerobic respiration
Glucose is not fully broken down
It does not need oxygen
teach.note: Ask: what if your muscles are working so hard that blood cannot deliver enough oxygen? They switch to anaerobic respiration as a temporary measure. Stress 'much less energy'; some books say about 2 ATP vs 30-32 ATP per glucose, but keep to 'much less' at KS3.

teach.heading: In muscles
bullets: glucose → lactic acid
Used during intense exercise like sprinting
Lactic acid builds up and muscles tire
After exercise, extra oxygen is needed (oxygen debt)
teach.note: Explain why we keep breathing hard after exercise: oxygen is needed to break down lactic acid. Misconception: lactic acid causes the sore muscles the next day. Research shows it does not; the soreness is from tiny muscle fibre damage. Keep the focus on fatigue during exercise.

teach.heading: In yeast: fermentation
bullets: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
Yeast is a single-celled fungus
Used in baking: the carbon dioxide makes dough rise
Ethanol evaporates when bread is baked
teach.note: Be sensitive: emphasise bread-making and biofuel (ethanol used as fuel) as the uses we discuss. Alcoholic drinks are haram and are not part of this lesson beyond noting that yeast fermentation is a natural process. Avoid detail on brewing.

teach.heading: Home yeast investigation
bullets: Mix yeast, warm water and sugar in a bottle
Fit a balloon over the neck
The balloon inflates as carbon dioxide is made
Variable to test: temperature, or amount of sugar
teach.note: Instruct pupils: use warm tap water (not hot), 1 teaspoon of yeast and 2 teaspoons of sugar. Make a prediction: which temperature gives the fastest rise? Discuss control variables. Safety: no tasting, wash hands after. Ask: why does a very hot temperature kill yeast? Enzymes denature.

teach.heading: Aerobic vs anaerobic
bullets: Aerobic: needs oxygen, releases lots of energy
Anaerobic: no oxygen, releases little energy
Aerobic makes carbon dioxide and water
Anaerobic makes lactic acid (muscle) or ethanol and CO2 (yeast)
teach.note: Complete a comparison table together. Ask: why can't we run a marathon using anaerobic respiration only? Because lactic acid builds up and we get tired quickly, and energy release is low. Athletes train to improve oxygen delivery so they can use aerobic respiration for longer.

practice: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
What substance builds up in muscles during anaerobic respiration?
Name the gas made by yeast that makes dough rise.
independent: Write word equations for anaerobic respiration in muscle and in yeast.
Complete a table comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration under four headings.
Explain why a sprinter keeps breathing heavily after finishing a race.
In the yeast experiment, balloons at 20°C, 35°C and 70°C inflate by different amounts. Predict and explain the results.
exit: Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy?
What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
lessons.homework: Carry out the yeast and balloon investigation with an adult, record balloon size after 20 minutes and write a conclusion.
lessons.send: SEND: comparison table partly filled in. EAL: pre-teach 'aerobic' (with air) and 'anaerobic' (without air). Stretch: explain why yeast can respire both aerobically and anaerobically.

lessons.title: Neutralisation and making salts
objectives: Describe neutralisation as acid + alkali → salt + water
Name the salts made from common acids
Predict the products of acid + metal and acid + carbonate reactions

keywords.def: a reaction between an acid and an alkali that makes a salt and water
a compound made when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal
a solution with a pH of 7
a compound containing carbon and oxygen, like calcium carbonate

starter: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
Name an indicator and its colour in an alkali.
Balance: H2 + Cl2 → HCl.

teach.heading: Neutralisation
bullets: Acid + alkali → salt + water
pH moves towards 7
Example: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water
The salt made is sodium chloride, common salt
teach.note: Draw a pH scale showing an acid becoming neutral as alkali is added. Misconception: all salts are table salt. Salt is a general name for compounds made from acids. Show a video of universal indicator changing colour as an alkali is added to an acid; do not use these chemicals at home.

teach.heading: Naming salts
bullets: Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides
Sulfuric acid makes sulfates
Nitric acid makes nitrates
The first part of the name comes from the metal
teach.note: Practise: sulfuric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium sulfate + water; nitric acid + potassium hydroxide → potassium nitrate + water. Ask pupils to complete the pattern for hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide. Make a three-column table to use as a reference.

teach.heading: Acid + metal
bullets: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen
Magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
Bubbles of hydrogen are seen
Test for hydrogen: a lit splint gives a squeaky pop
teach.note: Show a video of magnesium ribbon fizzing in dilute acid, then a squeaky pop test. Safety: hydrogen is flammable. Link to the reactivity series in lesson 14. Ask: why do copper and gold not react with dilute acid? Because they are unreactive.

teach.heading: Acid + carbonate
bullets: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide
Calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
Test for carbon dioxide: limewater turns cloudy
Limestone and marble are damaged by acid rain
teach.note: Home link: vinegar on chalk or on eggshell, which are both calcium carbonate: bubbles of carbon dioxide appear. Pupils record observations. Ask: how does this explain damage to limestone buildings by acid rain? Also link to antacid tablets that contain carbonates.

teach.heading: Neutralisation in real life
bullets: Antacids relieve indigestion
Lime is added to acidic soils and lakes
Toothpaste neutralises acids made by bacteria
Strong alkalis such as drain cleaner are never used as medicines
teach.note: Discuss the use of neutralisation for farmers and in medicine. Ask: why can't we use a strong alkali such as drain cleaner to treat indigestion? Because it is corrosive. Pupils evaluate which substances are suitable and why. Avoid medical advice beyond the science.

practice: Complete: acid + alkali → ________ + water.
Which acid makes sulfate salts?
What is the test for carbon dioxide gas?
independent: Write word equations for: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide; sulfuric acid + magnesium; nitric acid + calcium carbonate.
Name the salt made from each reaction in question 1.
Explain how an indigestion tablet works.
A farmer's soil has pH 5. Suggest a substance to add and explain what happens to the pH.
exit: Write the general equation for acid + alkali.
What gas is made when an acid reacts with a metal?
lessons.homework: Put a piece of chalk or an eggshell in vinegar and record what happens; write a word equation for the reaction.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence frames and a table of acid-to-salt names. EAL: key terms with images. Stretch: write balanced symbol equations for the reactions of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide and with magnesium.

lessons.title: Friction, air resistance and drag
objectives: Explain how friction and drag act against motion
Describe where friction is useful and where it is a problem
Explain streamlining and terminal velocity qualitatively

keywords.def: a contact force that opposes motion between two surfaces
friction between an object and the air as it moves through it
the resistive force on an object moving through a fluid
the steady speed reached when forces are balanced

starter: Define a resultant force.
What is the resultant force on a car travelling at a steady speed?
State Newton's first law in your own words.

teach.heading: What is friction?
bullets: Friction is a force between surfaces in contact
It acts in the opposite direction to motion
It changes kinetic energy into heat
Rougher surfaces produce more friction
teach.note: Pupils rub their hands together and feel warmth. Ask: where did the energy come from? Kinetic energy has been transferred to thermal energy. Compare ice, carpet and sandpaper. Misconception: friction only matters when objects are moving; static friction stops objects from sliding too.

teach.heading: Useful and harmful friction
bullets: Useful: brakes, grip on shoes, tyres, holding a pen
Harmful: wear on parts, wasted energy, heating
Reduce with oil, grease, ball bearings, smooth surfaces
Increase with treads, rough grips, rubber
teach.note: Make a table with both columns and ask for more examples. Discuss how prayer mats grip the floor and stop us slipping. Ask: how do mechanics reduce friction in engines? (Lubricating oil). Ask: how do race cars use friction? (Slick tyres with warm rubber grip better).

teach.heading: Air resistance and drag
bullets: Objects moving through air or water feel a resistive force
Drag increases with speed
Larger area gives more drag
Streamlined shapes reduce drag
teach.note: Demonstrate with two paper sheets, one flat, one scrunched, dropped together. Ask: why does the flat one fall slower? More area, more air resistance. Show images of a cyclist in a racing tuck and a dolphin shape. Pupils suggest design features that reduce drag in cars and aeroplanes.

teach.heading: Falling objects and terminal velocity
bullets: At the start: weight is greater than air resistance
Speed increases, so air resistance increases
Eventually weight equals air resistance
Resultant is 0 N, so speed stays constant
teach.note: Draw force arrows at four stages of a skydiver's fall; opening the parachute makes drag larger, so the skydiver slows, until a new smaller terminal velocity. Misconception: heavier objects always fall faster. In a vacuum all fall together; in air, drag matters. Ask pupils to explain why a feather falls slowly.

teach.heading: Investigating friction
bullets: Pull a block across different surfaces with a newton meter
Record the force just to keep it moving
Repeat three times and calculate the mean
Control: same block, same mass, same speed
teach.note: Home version: use a bag of rice on a string and a kitchen scale/spring balance or measure the angle at which a block starts to slide on a tilted board. Ask pupils to identify the independent, dependent and control variables. They must record results in a table and decide which surface has most friction.

practice: What direction does friction act relative to motion?
Give one example where friction is useful.
What happens to air resistance as a falling object speeds up?
independent: Draw force diagrams for a car accelerating, at constant speed and braking.
Describe the motion of a skydiver from jumping out of a plane to landing, using the terms weight, air resistance and terminal velocity.
Explain why cyclists crouch down in a race.
A block needs 4 N, 6 N and 3 N to move on surfaces A, B and C. Which has the most friction? Explain.
exit: State two ways to reduce friction.
What is the resultant force on a skydiver at terminal velocity?
lessons.homework: Investigate which surface in your home gives the most friction for a toy car or a shoe and record your results in a table.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn force diagrams with missing labels. EAL: key vocabulary 'grip', 'streamlined' with pictures. Stretch: explain why a parachute reaches a smaller terminal velocity than a freefalling skydiver.

lessons.title: Exercise, fitness and smoking
objectives: Describe how breathing and heart rate change during exercise and why
Explain how smoking damages the breathing system
Describe asthma and how it affects breathing

keywords.def: the number of times the heart beats per minute
how well the body can carry out physical activity
tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus away
a condition in which the airways become narrow and make breathing difficult

starter: What is aerobic respiration?
Why does anaerobic respiration make muscles tired?
Name the tiny air sacs in the lungs.

teach.heading: Exercise and the body
bullets: Muscles need more energy, so they need more oxygen
Breathing rate and depth increase
Heart rate rises to pump blood faster
Carbon dioxide is removed more quickly
teach.note: Practical (if healthy): pupils take their pulse for 15 s at rest and multiply by four; do one minute of star jumps; take pulse again and then each minute until it returns to normal. Anyone with a health condition should watch. Ask: why is recovery time a measure of fitness? A fitter heart recovers faster.

teach.heading: Fitness and training
bullets: Regular exercise strengthens the heart
Lungs take in more air per breath
Fit people have lower resting heart rates
Recovery time is shorter
teach.note: Plot data in a table for a fit and unfit person (resting 60 vs 80 bpm; recovery 2 vs 5 min). Ask pupils to conclude with evidence. Reflect on caring for the body as a trust (amanah): the hadith in Sahih Muslim says the strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, while there is good in both. Use it only as a reflection on strength and health.

teach.heading: What is in cigarette smoke?
bullets: Nicotine is addictive
Tar is a sticky substance that causes cancer
Carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried by the blood
Smoke contains many other harmful chemicals
teach.note: Be sensitive and factual. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen, so less oxygen reaches cells. Smoking is also a financial waste and, according to many scholars, impermissible due to harm. Qur'an 2:195 says do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands. Link to protecting the self.

teach.heading: How smoking damages the lungs
bullets: Cilia are damaged, so mucus and dirt build up
Smoker's cough and infections become more likely
Alveoli walls break down in emphysema
Tar can cause lung cancer
teach.note: Use a diagram of a healthy airway versus a smoker's airway. Ask: how do cilia protect the lungs? Make the link between less surface area and breathlessness from lesson 4. Mention that passive smoking also harms others, particularly children.

teach.heading: Asthma
bullets: Airways become inflamed and narrow
Triggers: pollen, dust, cold air, exercise, smoke
Symptoms: wheezing, tight chest, coughing
Reliever inhalers relax the muscles around the airways
teach.note: Be sensitive to pupils who have asthma. Explain that it is a long-term condition that can be managed. Asthma cannot be caught from others. Ask: why does smoke make asthma worse? Pupils create a leaflet outline on helping someone having an asthma attack: sit upright, use reliever inhaler, call for help if no improvement.

practice: Why does heart rate increase during exercise?
Name the gas that reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.
What are cilia?
independent: Plot or tabulate results of resting, exercise and recovery pulse rates for two people and conclude who is fitter.
Explain, using alveoli, why emphysema causes breathlessness.
Describe three ways cigarette smoke damages the breathing system.
Write advice to a friend who has asthma on managing exercise.
exit: Give two changes in the body during exercise.
Explain how smoking damages cilia.
lessons.homework: Create a poster titled 'Looking after my lungs' with five facts from this lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: pulse recording table provided. EAL: pre-teach 'inhaler' and 'wheeze'. Stretch: explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous even in small amounts.

lessons.title: The reactivity series and displacement
objectives: Order metals by how reactive they are using reactions with water, acid and oxygen
Explain what a displacement reaction is
Predict whether a displacement reaction will happen

keywords.def: a list of metals in order of how reactive they are
a reaction where a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one
a compound of an element with oxygen
the slow destruction of a metal by chemical reaction, such as rusting

starter: Name the gas made when a metal reacts with acid.
State the test for hydrogen.
Write the word equation for magnesium burning in oxygen.

teach.heading: Metals and oxygen
bullets: Metals react with oxygen to make metal oxides
Magnesium burns with a bright white flame
Gold does not react with oxygen
More reactive metals react faster
teach.note: Show videos of magnesium, iron wool and copper in a flame. Metal + oxygen → metal oxide. Ask pupils to say which is most reactive. Safety: do not look directly at the burning magnesium. Misconception: rusting and burning are the same; rusting is slow oxidation of iron with water and oxygen.

teach.heading: Metals with water and acid
bullets: Potassium, sodium and lithium react vigorously with cold water
Calcium reacts steadily; magnesium reacts slowly
Reaction with acid gives a salt and hydrogen
Copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute acid
teach.note: Show video of sodium in water: it fizzes and moves around, with hydrogen made. These metals are stored under oil. Ask: why does the order of bubbling speed give the order of reactivity? Faster bubbles mean a more reactive metal. Remind pupils of the hydrogen pop test.

teach.heading: The reactivity series
bullets: Potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium
Aluminium, zinc, iron, copper
Silver, gold at the bottom
Order: most reactive at the top
teach.note: Provide the list on the board, and a mnemonic, such as 'Please Stop Lying, Calling Me A Zebra, I Can Sing Gospel' to help pupils. Pupils create their own mnemonic. Note that carbon and hydrogen are often included for comparison. Ask: why are gold and silver used in jewellery? They are unreactive and stay shiny.

teach.heading: Displacement reactions
bullets: A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive one
Iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper
Magnesium + zinc sulfate → magnesium sulfate + zinc
No reaction if the added metal is less reactive
teach.note: Video: an iron nail in blue copper sulfate solution becomes coated in pinkish copper and the solution fades. Ask: why did iron displace copper? Iron is more reactive. Pupils predict: will copper displace magnesium from magnesium sulfate? No. Copper sulfate is a hazardous chemical, so only demonstrate by video.

teach.heading: Using the reactivity series
bullets: Unreactive metals are found uncombined in the ground (gold)
Reactive metals are extracted by electrolysis (later)
Metals like iron can be extracted using carbon
Aluminium is used in cans because it is protected by an oxide layer
teach.note: Link to Earth's resources from Year 8. Ask: why is iron cheaper than aluminium to extract? Carbon can displace iron from iron oxide but not aluminium, which needs electrolysis. This gives a taste of GCSE chemistry. Mention that using metals sustainably and recycling them is part of our role as stewards (khalifah) of the Earth.

practice: Put these in order of reactivity: copper, magnesium, gold, zinc.
What gas is made when sodium reacts with water?
Write a general word equation for a metal reacting with oxygen.
independent: Predict yes or no and write a word equation for: zinc + copper sulfate; copper + zinc sulfate; magnesium + iron sulfate.
Explain why potassium is stored under oil.
A student places a piece of copper in silver nitrate solution and silver crystals form. What does this show?
Create your own mnemonic for the reactivity series and use it to order eight metals.
exit: What is a displacement reaction?
Will silver displace iron from iron sulfate? Explain.
lessons.homework: Research the use of two metals (one reactive, one unreactive) and explain how their reactivity affects how they are used.
lessons.send: SEND: reactivity series card with a prediction flow chart. EAL: key term cards 'react', 'displace'. Stretch: explain why aluminium does not react with water in everyday use despite being reactive.

lessons.title: Gravity, mass and weight
objectives: Distinguish mass from weight and give units
Use W = m × g to calculate weight
Compare weight on Earth, the Moon and other planets

keywords.def: the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg
the force of gravity on an object, measured in newtons
the force of gravity on each kilogram, in N/kg
the force of attraction between masses

starter: Give two examples of non-contact forces.
What is the unit of force?
Describe the motion of a skydiver at terminal velocity.

teach.heading: What is gravity?
bullets: Gravity is a force of attraction between masses
Bigger mass means stronger gravity
It keeps us on the Earth and the Moon in orbit
Gravity acts at a distance
teach.note: Ask: why do we feel the Earth's gravity but not the pull of a table? Because the Earth is so massive. Introduce that the Earth and Moon pull on each other. Qur'an 67:3-4 invites us to look at the creation and find no flaw; the order of the heavens is one sign of design.

teach.heading: Mass and weight
bullets: Mass: amount of matter, in kilograms (kg)
Weight: force of gravity, in newtons (N)
Mass stays the same everywhere
Weight changes with gravity
teach.note: Misconception: mass and weight are the same thing. In everyday speech 'weight' is used for mass in kg. Use a bathroom scale: it measures weight but displays kg. Ask: if you went to the Moon, what happens to your mass and weight? Mass is the same; weight is lower.

teach.heading: W = m × g
bullets: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength
On Earth g is about 10 N/kg (9.8 N/kg exactly)
Example: 60 kg × 10 N/kg = 600 N
Newton meters measure weight
teach.note: Write the equation triangle. Work through: a 2.5 kg bag of rice weighs 25 N; an astronaut with weight 700 N has mass 70 kg. Show rearrangements m = W ÷ g. Use g = 10 N/kg for ease and mention 9.8 N/kg will be used later in GCSE. Insist on units.

teach.heading: Other planets and the Moon
bullets: Moon: g = 1.6 N/kg
Mars: g = 3.7 N/kg
Jupiter: g = 25 N/kg
A 50 kg pupil weighs 500 N on Earth, 80 N on the Moon
teach.note: Calculate: the same pupil on Mars weighs 50 × 3.7 = 185 N and on Jupiter 50 × 25 = 1250 N. Ask why the Moon's gravity is weaker (less mass). Misconception: there is no gravity in space; astronauts float because they are in free fall around Earth. Values are rounded; Jupiter's is about 24.8 N/kg.

teach.heading: Using the equation
bullets: Find the mass if weight is 450 N on Earth
Find the weight of a 0.2 kg phone: 2 N
Check units and size: does it make sense?
teach.note: Run a quick plenary with mini-whiteboards. Real-life reasoning: an apple weighs about 1 N. Ask pupils to estimate the weight of a laptop (about 20 N for 2 kg). Reinforce that a 1 kg bag of flour weighs about 10 N on Earth, so it is not 1 N.

practice: What is the unit of mass? What is the unit of weight?
What is the weight of a 5 kg mass on Earth (g = 10 N/kg)?
Does mass change on the Moon?
independent: Calculate the weight on Earth of: 3 kg, 0.5 kg and 80 kg masses.
Calculate the mass of an object that weighs 250 N on Earth.
Complete a table of weights for a 40 kg pupil on Earth, Moon, Mars, Jupiter.
Explain why astronauts seem weightless on the International Space Station.
exit: Write the equation linking weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
A 12 kg object is on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). What is its weight?
lessons.homework: Weigh or estimate the mass of five household objects and calculate their weights in newtons on Earth and on the Moon.
lessons.send: SEND: formula triangle with units and example. EAL: pre-teach 'mass', 'weight', and 'field'. Stretch: explain why g is greater on Jupiter than on the Moon using mass and radius.

lessons.title: Pressure
objectives: Define pressure and use p = F ÷ A
Explain how area changes pressure in everyday examples
Describe how pressure in liquids and gases changes

keywords.def: the force acting on each unit of area
the unit of pressure (Pa), equal to one newton per square metre
the amount of surface, in square metres or square centimetres
a liquid or a gas

starter: Calculate the weight of a 30 kg mass (g = 10 N/kg).
What is the area of a rectangle 0.5 m by 0.2 m?
Why are skis wide?

teach.heading: What is pressure?
bullets: Pressure depends on force and area
pressure = force ÷ area
Unit: pascal (Pa) = N/m²
Small area gives high pressure
teach.note: Use two demonstrations: pushing a finger against a balloon vs a pin. Same force, different area. Ask which makes a hole. Explain why a sharp knife cuts better. Misconception: pressure and force are the same thing. Pressure is the effect of the force spread over an area.

teach.heading: Pressure calculations
bullets: Worked example: 600 N on 0.02 m²
Rearrange: F = p × A; A = F ÷ p
Convert cm² to m²: divide by 10 000
teach.note: Another example: an elephant with weight 40 000 N standing on four feet, each 0.1 m² (total 0.4 m²): p = 100 000 Pa. A girl in high heels with weight 500 N and heel area 0.0005 m²: p = 1 000 000 Pa, ten times the elephant! Pupils are often surprised. Give plenty of practice with units.

teach.heading: Everyday pressure
bullets: Increase pressure: knives, nails, drawing pins
Decrease pressure: skis, snowshoes, tractor tyres
Camels have wide feet for sand
Spread the force over a bigger area
teach.note: Ask pupils to sort items by whether they are designed to give high or low pressure. The camel's feet are an example of adaptation in the creation; avoid religious claims beyond noting design. Link back to forces and weight: a heavier person gives more pressure.

teach.heading: Pressure in liquids
bullets: Pressure increases with depth
Liquids press in all directions
Dams are thicker at the bottom
Deep sea divers feel more pressure
teach.note: Demonstrate with a bottle with holes at different heights (video): the bottom jet shoots furthest. Explain that more water above means more weight pressing down. Misconception: liquids press only downwards. Ask: why do submarines need strong hulls?

teach.heading: Pressure in gases
bullets: Gas pressure comes from particles hitting surfaces
More collisions give higher pressure
Heating gas or squeezing it into a smaller volume raises pressure
Atmospheric pressure decreases with height
teach.note: Link to particle model from KS3. Ask: why does a tyre feel harder after a long drive? Particles move faster and hit the walls harder when heated. Why do our ears pop on a plane? The pressure outside falls with altitude. Use a quick drawing of particles in a syringe.

practice: Write the equation for pressure.
What is the unit of pressure?
Why is it easier to push a sharp drawing pin than a blunt one?
independent: Calculate the pressure when 200 N acts on 0.5 m².
A 60 kg person has feet area 0.04 m² in total. Calculate the pressure on the ground (g = 10 N/kg).
Calculate the pressure from a 500 N person standing on one foot, 0.015 m², and on both feet.
Explain why tractors have wide tyres.
exit: A force of 50 N acts on an area of 0.25 m². Calculate the pressure.
Explain why a knife with a sharp edge cuts more easily.
lessons.homework: Find three examples at home where pressure is increased or reduced by changing the area and explain each one.
lessons.send: SEND: worked calculation frame with steps. EAL: pre-teach 'area' and 'spread'. Stretch: derive the pressure at the bottom of a 2 m deep tank using weight of water, or explain why pressure in a liquid is the same in all directions.
